The licensing business has near-zero marginal costs, generating extremely high margins. The chip business relies on massive fixed R&D investments while outsourcing manufacturing (variable COGS) to foundries like TSMC. This structure creates high operating leverage, as revenue growth scales efficiently against the fixed R&D base.
forensic_report.moat_evidence: Qualcomm's wide moat is primarily driven by its intangible assets—specifically its massive portfolio of standard-essential patents (SEPs) for 3G, 4G, and 5G technologies. Its QTL segment collects royalties on nearly every smartphone sold globally. Additionally, its QCT segment benefits from high switching costs due to the deep integration of its Snapdragon processors and modems into OEM device architectures, making it difficult for Android manufacturers to switch without significant redesigns.
forensic_report.pricing_power_evidence: Qualcomm extracts a percentage of the total selling price of smartphones for its licensing (though capped at a certain device value), effectively giving it pricing power as premium device prices rise. forensic_report.concentration_details: Qualcomm faces significant customer and supplier concentration risks.
